extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting patent claim language during USPTO examination, addressing the broadest reasonable interpretation standard, plain meaning, preamble effect, transitional phrases, lexicography, and related evidentiary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification (i.e., construed as broadly as their terms reasonably allow, taking into account the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI reduces the chance that an issued claim will later be interpreted more broadly than justified; applicants can amend claims during prosecution, so the PTO applies BRI rather than the narrower claim construction used in infringement suits. Case law examples: Phillips, In re American Academy of Sci. Tech. Ctr., In re Yamamoto, In re Zletz, In re Morris. Ensure interpretation remains reasonable and consistent with how skilled artisans would understand the claim in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim words given plain meaning unless inconsistent with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, claim terms are given their ordinary and customary (plain) meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, unless that meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary and customary meaning is evidenced by claim language, specification, drawings, prior art, and the best source is the specification (which can serve as a glossary). If the specification conflicts with the plain meaning, the specification controls. Example: Chef America v. Lamb‑Weston (ordinary English words construed as written).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to read limitations from the specification into a claim—preferred embodiments or specific examples in the written description should not be used to narrow claim scope unless the claim language itself requires it or there is a clear disavowal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reading a single embodiment's details into broader claim language. Case examples: Superguide, Liebel‑Flarsheim, In re Zletz, In re Marosi. Exception: when claim language falls under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph (means/step-plus-function), the specification must be consulted to determine corresponding structure/material/acts. When ambiguity exists, consult the intrinsic record to decide if a limitation is implicitly required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation must be consistent with how a person of ordinary skill would construe terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation must also accord with the interpretation that those skilled in the art would reach in light of the intrinsic record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt an interpretation that, though broad, would be unreasonable to a skilled artisan. Use art-specific knowledge and analogous usage to ensure reasonableness. Case examples: In re Cortright (construing 'restore hair growth' to mean some increase, not necessarily full restoration), In re Buszard (distinguishing flexible vs. rigid foam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources to determine ordinary and customary meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term may be evidenced by the words of the claims, the specification, drawings, prosecution history, prior art, and extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, technical treatises, expert testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extrinsic sources give multiple definitions, consult the intrinsic record to select the meaning most consistent with the applicant's use. Dictionaries and other references must be compared against the context in the specification. Case examples: Phillips, Ferguson Beauregard/Logic Controls, Renishaw, Vitronics, Brookhill‑Wilk, Rexnord, Toro.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-as-lexicographer (special definitions by applicant)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may act as his/her own lexicographer and define a term differently from its ordinary meaning, but must do so with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision in the specification so that one of ordinary skill in the art is put on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit definitions in the specification control claim interpretation. Implicit definitions by consistent usage in the specification may also define terms. The special meaning must be sufficiently clear to justify departure from common usage. Case examples: In re Paulsen, Multiform Desiccants, Merck v. Teva (failure to clearly redefine 'about'). See MPEP § 2173.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of preamble determined case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether preamble language limits claim scope depends on the entire record; there is no single litmus test—preamble may be limiting when it supplies essential structure/steps or gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim, but non-limiting when it merely states purpose or intended use and the claim body is structurally complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If preamble language recites structural limitations, it should be treated as part of the claimed invention (Corning Glass Works, Pac‑Tec, In re Stencel). If the preamble only states purpose and deletion does not affect claim structure, it is generally not limiting (Pitney Bowes, Rowe v. Dror). Evaluate whether the preamble was relied upon during prosecution to distinguish prior art—clear reliance can transform the preamble into a limitation (Catalina, Metabolite Labs.). Use prosecution history and specification to determine whether the preamble provides context or a limiting feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble statements that limit structure vs. statements of purpose/intended use
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble terminology that limits the structure of the claimed invention functions as a claim limitation; preamble recitations of purpose or intended use generally do not limit the claim unless they result in a structural/manipulative difference or were relied upon during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the body of the claim intrinsically sets forth all limitations; if so, the preamble likely is non-limiting. If the preamble supplies essential characterizing structure or the prosecution history shows reliance on the preamble to distinguish prior art, treat it as limiting. Case examples: Corning, Pitney Bowes, Jansen, In re Otto, In re Cruciferous Sprout Litig., Poly‑America, Intirtool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases define openness/closedness of claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases such as 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', and 'consisting of' affect whether additional, unrecited elements or steps are excluded; determination is fact-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Comprising' (including/containing/characterized by) is presumptively open-ended and allows additional elements or steps (e.g., method claims using 'comprising' are open). 'Consisting of' and 'consisting essentially of' signal more closed scope; 'group consisting of' often indicates a closed Markush group. Case examples: Mars v. H.J. Heinz, Invitrogen v. Biocrest, Genentech v. Chiron, Gillette v. Energizer, In re Baxter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim terms are ambiguous, consult the specification for the inventor's meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim term is ambiguous, the specification should be consulted to determine the meaning ascribed to that term by the inventor; the specification may define ambiguous terms or point away from improper meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification to clarify ambiguous terms rather than importing extraneous limitations. Case examples: In re Weiss (look to specification-defined meaning for 'preselected level of force'), Renishaw (disqualifying improper dictionary meanings inconsistent with intrinsic record), Rapoport v. Dement (distinguishing treatment vs. secondary symptoms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means/step-plus-function claim elements require specification for corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When an element is claimed using means-plus-function or step-plus-function language (35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph), the specification must be consulted to determine the structure, material, or acts corresponding to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the corresponding structure disclosed in the specification that performs the recited function; failure to identify adequate corresponding structure can affect statutory subject matter/definiteness. Case example: In re Donaldson; see MPEP §§ 2181–2186 and § 2173.05(a).
